title: Gasoline isn’t really that expensive
gist: Yglesias argues that by historical standards the 2026 US economy (3.7% inflation, 4.1% unemployment, solid GDP) and gasoline prices are not that bad, and that voter rage driving the biggest midterm wave since 1974 is better explained by a 'betrayal' theory: neither Biden nor Trump, nor Democratic think tanks, has genuinely prioritized inflation reduction over five years of elevated inflation.

insights.claim: US CPI inflation was 3.7 percent as of September 2026, versus over 12 percent in 1974 and 7 percent in 2021 and 6.5 percent in 2022.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Inflation is well above the 2% target but far from crisis levels; persistent above-target prints keep rate-cut expectations constrained.
insights.quote: As of September, it was 3.7 percent.
insights.locator: Voters, clearly, are very upset

insights.claim: The 2026 midterms were the biggest midterm wave election since 1974, with cost of living a central factor.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A Democratic Congress with an affordability mandate will shape 2027-28 fiscal, trade and regulatory policy.
insights.quote: This was the biggest midterm wave since 1974.
insights.locator: Voters, clearly, are very upset

insights.claim: More than 70 percent of Latino voters in Texas cited cost of living as a top-three issue, versus roughly 35 percent for immigration and border security.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Cost of living dominates even among demographics assumed to vote on immigration; policy will chase price relief.
insights.quote: more than 70 percent of those voters cite the cost of living as a top three issue compared with roughly 35 percent for immigration and border security
insights.locator: Voters, clearly, are very upset

insights.claim: The US labor market looks well balanced: unemployment is low at 4.1 percent, GDP growth is solid, and the job openings rate slightly exceeds the unemployment rate, per Jason Furman's dashboard.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Tight labor market with sticky inflation argues against stimulus and for continued restrictive rates.
insights.quote: The unemployment rate is low at 4.1 percent and has been low for a long time.

insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Fuel-price political salience exceeds its real economic burden; demand destruction risk from current prices is limited.

insights.claim: Beef has become unprecedentedly expensive, less affordable now than in the 1980s, while chicken is cheaper.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Protein substitution from beef to chicken is a consumer-staples trend to watch.
insights.quote: Beef is way less affordable right now than it was in the 1980s, but chicken is cheaper.

insights.claim: Voter rage is best explained by a sense of betrayal: after the 2021-22 inflation surge, neither party ever made a strong policy pivot to fighting inflation, and the US is now in year five of the inflationary episode.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Expect political pressure for visible anti-inflation policy; parties that fail to deliver will keep being punished.
insights.quote: we’re now on Year Five of the inflationary episode and first Democrats and now Republicans have declined to genuinely prioritize inflation reduction
insights.locator: How sure am I that this

insights.claim: Trump increased the budget deficit in a way that added inflationary pressure, and his war with Iran produced a negative supply shock that re-accelerated inflation.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Fiscal expansion plus an energy supply shock supports higher-for-longer rates and term premium.
insights.quote: he increased the budget deficit in a way that increased inflationary pressures, and then we got a negative supply shock when he started a war with Iran
insights.locator: Then Trump won promising

insights.claim: Trump's tariff agenda is premised on higher prices protecting US manufacturers, and his immigration policy deliberately shrinks the workforce, both of which push against lower inflation.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Tariffs and labor-supply constraints are structural inflation drivers; watch labor-intensive sectors' wage pressure.
insights.quote: the whole premise of the tariff agenda is that higher prices are a good idea because you’re trying to protect American manufacturers from low-cost competition
insights.locator: Of course, Trump is president right now

insights.claim: The Biden economic team, when asked, could name no cost-of-living policy they adopted specifically because of inflation that they would not otherwise have favored.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Illustrates absence of genuine inflation-driven policy shifts in Washington.
insights.quote: And they legitimately had nothing to offer.

insights.claim: Unlike in 2008, 2009 and the Covid CARES Act, when parties collaborated on responses to economic problems, political elites have not altered policy priorities at all in response to the inflation problem.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Lack of bipartisan anti-inflation action means monetary policy continues to bear the burden.
insights.quote: the answer is genuinely not at all
insights.locator: A crisis of politics, not economics

insights.claim: Democratic-aligned think tanks have rebranded off-the-shelf 2019 ideas — neo-Brandeisian antitrust, expanded child-care subsidies, climate policy — as affordability policy instead of retooling an agenda to reduce inflation and interest rates.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A 2029 Democratic agenda may still lack disinflationary substance; Yglesias urges a pivot that would favor deregulation and fiscal restraint.
insights.quote: everyone has taken the same off-the-shelf ideas from 2019 — neo-Brandeisian antitrust policy, expanded child-care subsidies, fighting climate change — and given them an affordability rebrand

insights.claim: When consumers are angry about prices, antitrust should pivot back toward the consumer-welfare school emphasizing low consumer prices, away from Lina Khan's neo-Brandeisian approach.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A shift back to consumer-price-focused antitrust would ease merger risk for large firms.
insights.quote: when everyone is mad about consumer prices, you pivot back to the “low consumer prices are really important” school of thought

insights.claim: Funding new spending via wealth taxes or taxes on unrealized capital gains is inflationary because it increases overall consumption.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Wealth-tax-funded spending proposals would add to demand-side inflation pressure.
insights.quote: Taxing wealth or unrealized capital gains is an inflationary mechanism of financing new government spending

insights.claim: Political scientist Christoffer Dausgaard found, using local variation in gasoline prices, that the swing against Republicans was not larger where gas prices rose more than average.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Voter anger is national and sociotropic, not tied to local price levels; local price relief won't buy votes.
insights.quote: the level of public anger about prices does not vary with the prices themselves
insights.locator: Political scientist Christoffer Dausgaard

insights.claim: Democrats won Senate and gubernatorial races in oil-producing Alaska and Texas, where a Middle East energy shock arguably helps the local economy, showing anger was uniform rather than tied to local economic impact.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Even energy-state voters punished incumbents' party; energy windfalls don't insulate politicians.
insights.quote: Democrats are winning the Senate and gubernatorial races in both those states
insights.locator: One piece of evidence for this view

insights.claim: Northern New England is more exposed to the Strait of Hormuz shock due to heating-oil reliance and LNG-dependent gas power plants, yet its swing against Republicans matched the national pattern, and Republican governors in New Hampshire and Vermont were re-elected.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: New England energy prices are especially sensitive to Hormuz/LNG disruptions — a regional utility and heating-oil exposure.

insights.claim: Cindy Hyde-Smith's remark that people can switch proteins if beef is too expensive was so politically toxic it apparently helped elect a Democrat in Mississippi.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Dismissing price complaints is electorally lethal; expect politicians to push visible food-price measures.
